title: How Does the Internet Cross the Ocean?
sources: TeleGeography Submarine Cable FAQ / Tim Stronge congressional testimony: submarine cables carry about 99% of intercontinental data traffic; satellites carry a tiny share
TeleGeography Submarine Cable Map 2025: roughly 600 active and planned cable systems; about 1.4-1.5 million km of cable in service

TeleGeography FAQ / Kentik 'Diving Deep into Submarine Cables' / EarthDate 'Light Speed, Under the Sea': deep-sea cables are about the diameter of a garden hose (~17-21 mm); shallow sections near shore are armoured and thicker
Kentik / Fujikura: inside are hair-thin optical glass fibres carrying data as pulses of laser light; repeaters spaced every ~50-100 km amplify the light so it can cross thousands of km

ICPC 'Sharks are not the Nemesis of the Internet' / Computerworld: sharks have bitten cables (footage published, Google added protective sheathing in 2014) but fish bites are a tiny fraction of faults
ICPC media FAQ: about 150-200 cable faults a year, most (around 70-80%) caused by fishing gear and ship anchors

lines.text: How does the internet get across an ocean?
almost all of it runs through cables
lying right on the sea floor.
Hundreds of them stretch over a million kilometres,
and way down deep, they're only as thick as a garden hose.
lines.caps: AND WAY *DOWN | *DEEP | THEY'RE *ONLY | AS *THICK | AS A *GARDEN | *HOSE

lines.text: Inside are hair-thin strands of glass,
and your messages zip through them as flashes of light.
lines.caps: AND YOUR *MESSAGES | ZIP *THROUGH | THEM AS *FLASHES | OF *LIGHT

lines.text: Every so often, a repeater boosts the light,
so it can cross a whole ocean.
Here's the twist: sharks have actually bitten these cables!
But the real villains are fishing nets and ship anchors.
lines.caps: BUT THE *REAL | *VILLAINS | ARE FISHING *NETS | AND SHIP *ANCHORS

lines.text: So that meme you just sent abroad probably went for a swim.
lines.caps: SO THAT *MEME | YOU JUST *SENT | *ABROAD | PROBABLY *WENT | FOR A *SWIM
